steps.title: Aggregate a set of rows
steps.content: Aggregate functions summarize many rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. GROUP BY creates a separate group for each distinct grouping key.
steps.example: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY department_id;

steps.title: Filter rows before grouping
steps.prompt: Which clause filters individual rows before groups are formed?
steps.explanation: WHERE filters rows before the grouping and aggregate calculation.

steps.title: Filter groups with HAVING
steps.content: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregate conditions. For example, HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 keeps departments with more than five employees.
steps.example: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM Employee GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

steps.title: Choose the aggregate filter
steps.prompt: You need departments whose average salary is above 50,000. Which clause should contain AVG(salary) > 50000?
steps.explanation: The condition is on a grouped aggregate, so it belongs in HAVING.

steps.title: Order of operations
steps.content: Conceptually, FROM and JOIN build rows, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT projects results, and ORDER BY sorts the output.
steps.tip: A column in SELECT normally needs to be grouped or aggregated when GROUP BY is used.

questions.prompt: Which function counts all result rows?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows with NULL values in some columns.

questions.prompt: Which clause forms groups by department?
questions.explanation: GROUP BY creates a group for each distinct department_id.

questions.prompt: Which clause filters groups with COUNT(*) > 3?
What is the main difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups
WHERE sorts rows; HAVING joins tables
questions.explanation: WHERE is applied to rows before grouping; HAVING applies to grouped results.

questions.prompt: Which query gets total sales per customer?
options: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM Sales GROUP BY customer_id
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM Sales WHERE customer_id
SELECT customer_id FROM Sales HAVING amount
SELECT customer_id, amount FROM Sales ORDER BY SUM
questions.explanation: Group by customer_id and sum amount for each group.
